title: PS-5 Effects of branched chain amino acid supplementation on complete blood cell counts of pre-weaned dairy calves following immune challenge
content:
Abstract
The objective was to determine the effects of branched chain amino acid supplementation on complete blood cell counts of pre-weaned dairy calves following a single intraperitoneal dose of lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Forty pre-weaned Holstein calves (42.5 ± 4.05 kg) were blocked by arrival date, stratified by body weight and serum total protein, and randomly assigned within block to 1 of 4 treatments arranged in a 2 x 2 factorial (n = 10 per treatment). The main effects were diet and immune challenge. Calves received (as a percentage of total milk solids) either 1) 1.0% L-Leu, 0.4% L-Val and 0.4% L-Ile (BCAA), or 2) 1.25% L-Ala as isonitrogenous control (ALA). Treatments were supplemented daily in milk replacer (20% CP 20% fat) for the 21-d experiment. The immune challenge on d 16 consisted of either a single intraperitoneal dose of LPS at 5 μg/kg BW (+LPS); or an intraperitoneal dose of saline (-LPS). Whole blood was collected at 0, 6, 12, 24 h relative to immune challenge. Data were analyzed in SAS using proc GLIMMIX, with fixed effects of diet, LPS, hour, and their interactions, and the random effect of block. The +LPS calves had increased levels of total white blood cells at h 12 and 24 relative to -LPS calves (LPS x h; P < 0.05). There was a decrease in lymphocytes and monocytes at h 6 for +LPS relative to -LPS calves (LPS x h; P < 0.05). There were no diet effects on these parameters. Neutrophils were higher for +LPS calves at h 12 and 24 relative to -LPS calves (LPS x h; P < 0.05). Neutrophils were lower for BCAA calves relative to ALA calves (diet; P < 0.05). The BCAA calves tended to have a higher percent of lymphocytes (diet; P = 0.089) and had a lower percent of neutrophils (diet; P < 0.05) relative to ALA calves. Among -LPS calves, BCAA calves had a greater percent of monocytes compared to ALA calves (diet x LPS; P < 0.05). There were no treatment or time effects for red blood cells or hematocrit. Platelets were lower for +LPS calves at h 6 and 12 compared to -LPS calves (LPS x h; P < 0.05). These results indicate that intraperitoneal LPS induced a systemic immune response that altered levels of circulating immune cells and platelets. These results also suggest that dietary amino acid supplementation altered immune cell counts in pre-weaned dairy calves, but that BCAA supplementation had minimal positive effects on complete blood cell counts following immune challenge.
